title: Editing & proofreading
examples: When I proofread, what should I look for first?
What is the difference between editing and proofreading?
Can you give me some tips for catching my own mistakes?

explain.say: Today we are learning about editing and proofreading your writing.

items: Editing fixes big ideas and structure.

explain.say: Editing means looking at the big picture of your writing.

items: Idea 2: Are the paragraphs organized well?

explain.say: A common error is using weak topic sentences in paragraphs.
Proofreading focuses on the small details like spelling and punctuation.
A common error is forgetting to check verb tense consistency.
In real life, you proofread a notice before posting it.

faq.q: What is the difference between editing and proofreading?
faq.a: Editing looks at the structure and main ideas of your writing. Proofreading looks for small mistakes like typos and punctuation errors.
asks: What should I do first when I review my essay?
Is editing about the words or the ideas?

faq.q: How many times should I proofread my work?
faq.a: It is best to read your work aloud several times. This helps you catch awkward phrasing and missed words.
asks: Should I wait until tomorrow to check my writing?
Does reading it out loud help catch errors?

faq.q: What is a strong topic sentence?
faq.a: A strong topic sentence clearly tells the reader what that whole paragraph will be about. It acts like a mini-thesis for that section.
asks: How do I make my topic sentence stronger?
Does the topic sentence need to be a question?

faq.q: What punctuation mark is most often forgotten?
faq.a: The comma is often forgotten when listing items or separating clauses. Remember to pause slightly when you read it.
asks: When do I use a semicolon?
Are there rules for commas after headings?

faq.q: Should I use a spell-checker program?
faq.a: Spell-checkers are helpful but not perfect. They will not catch misused words or grammatical errors.
asks: Are spell-checkers reliable for all words?
What if the word is spelled correctly but used wrong?

facts: Editing involves improving the content and organization of your writing.
Proofreading involves checking for surface errors like spelling and punctuation.
Reading your work aloud can help you hear mistakes you might overlook.
A topic sentence should introduce the main idea of a single paragraph.

quiz.say: The main idea of the entire essay is unclear.
quiz.why: This relates to the overall structure and content, which is the job of editing.

wrong.1: Proofreading only checks for small surface errors, not big ideas.
wrong.2: Grammar checking focuses on sentence rules, not the overall argument.
wrong.3: This is too narrow; spelling only covers one small part of the writing.

quiz.say: I wrote 'She run fast' instead of 'She ran fast'.
quiz.why: This is a mistake in verb tense that needs correcting during the review process.

wrong.0: This error is about the verb form, not the marks around it.
wrong.1: This error is within a sentence, not the guiding sentence for a paragraph.
wrong.3: The word 'ran' is spelled correctly, so this is not a spelling error.

quiz.say: When I review my work, I should read it slowly, pausing after every comma.
quiz.why: Reading aloud forces your brain to process every word and punctuation mark as if speaking.

wrong.0: Spell-checkers miss misused words that are spelled correctly.
wrong.1: While helpful, this is a person, not a technique you can always use.
wrong.2: Skipping parts means you will definitely miss errors in those sections.
